title: How to Secure Agents using OAuth — Jared Hanson (Keycard, Passport.js)
talk_summary: Jared Hanson explains OAuth roles (client, resource server, authorization server) and how MCP's authorization spec initially collapsed the authorization server into the MCP server, then was corrected to model MCP servers as pure resource servers that only verify tokens. He surveys future needs: agent identity via URL/PKI, client credentials for agent-to-agent, token exchange for chain of custody, and transactional authorization.

takeaways.technique: Separate authorization server from resource servers
takeaways.what_they_do: Model each MCP/tool server as an OAuth resource server that only verifies incoming tokens; a distinct authorization server handles consent, token issuance, and policy centrally.
takeaways.evidence_quote: All you have to do is verify the tokens that come in over HTTP and hand off all the other responsibility to the OA server.

takeaways.technique: Short-lived tokens with refresh rotation instead of static keys
takeaways.what_they_do: Use short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens so credentials rotate quickly while the authorized connection persists.
takeaways.evidence_quote: refresh tokens which basically allows these access tokens to be shortlived and rotated pretty quickly while still maintaining the the authorized connection

takeaways.what_they_do: Use the OAuth client credentials grant when an agent acts on its own behalf (not a user's) to call another agent or tool server.
takeaways.evidence_quote: client credentials and this applies when we want agents to communicate with other agents or other MCP servers on their own behalf not on behalf of a user

takeaways.technique: Token exchange for chain of custody
takeaways.what_they_do: Use OAuth token exchange so a downstream service gets a token derived from the caller's, preserving who originated the request across hops.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there's a technique called OOTH token exchange that I recommend everyone look into

takeaways.what_they_do: Skip uncredentialed dynamic client registration (makes agents anonymous); prefer public-client well-known identifiers or URL/PKI-based agent identity with signed assertions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it like makes all agents anonymous because the registration request itself is uncredentialed. This makes it hard to build trust in agents.
